title: Silhouette and Poppy
objective: Students will look closely at the exhibition’s two posters and see how few means they use: a **near-black ground**, **gray photographs**, **off-white type**, and **red** kept for the date, the hour and the poppies. They will study the **silhouette**, a figure without a face that can stand for every soldier, and three **symbols** of remembrance, then design a remembrance panel in which every choice has a reason.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: A poster has a few seconds to make a stranger stop and remember. Color, shape and symbol do that work before a single word is read.

items.text: describe how the two posters use a held-back palette, and where they spend their one red

materials: The two posters and the symbols on page 3, projected or printed in color
Pencils, black and gray markers or charcoal, and one red (crayon, pencil or paint)
connection: **Online,** open the two posters in the exhibition and watch the red date and time appear; then visit *The Memorial*. **In the exhibition,** stand in front of the backlit silhouette, and look at the Brodie helmet’s outline in the display case.

steps.title: A soldier with no face
script: Show the picture from the When the Guns Fell Silent poster: a soldier, a cross on a hill, red poppies. Ask: *“This soldier has no face. Why might an artist choose that?”* Students will notice the helmet, the rifle, the bowed head, and that we cannot tell who he is. *“Because he has no face, he could be anyone’s son. Today we look at how the posters make us remember, before we read a word.”*

screen.alt: A soldier in a helmet, a rifle on his back, silhouetted beside a wooden cross on a hill under a gray sky, with red poppies at the right

steps.purpose: Look before explaining: what does a silhouette hide, and what does it give?
students: This soldier has no face. Why might an artist choose that?
What can you still tell about him?

steps.title: Two posters, one palette
script: **Palette.** Put the two posters side by side. Students list the colors: near-black, gray, off-white, and red. The red is spent carefully: on the date **11.11.1918** and the time **11:00** on both posters, and on the poppies climbing the second. The photographs are sepia and gray. Ask what the red does to the eye.

items.alt: The Doughboys: America’s Sons in The Great War poster: a sepia photograph of four soldiers walking away down a ruined trench above the faded faces of soldiers in helmets, the title in off-white, three paragraphs of text, and the date 11.11.1918 and the time 11:00 in red
items.label: The Doughboys

items.alt: When the Guns Fell Silent at the 11th Hour poster: the date 11.11.1918 and the time 11:00 in red above four paragraphs of text, and the title over a photograph of a soldier silhouetted beside a wooden cross on a hill, with red poppies climbing the right edge
items.label: When the Guns Fell Silent

steps.purpose: See how little color the posters use, and where they put the red.
students: List every color you can see.
Where is the red? What does it mark?

steps.title: One figure for many
script: **Silhouette.** The figure in the When the Guns Fell Silent poster is a silhouette, and the Memorial room uses one against the sunset. In the exhibition, a backlit silhouette display stood beside the case, with soldier cards to take away. A silhouette keeps the outline (helmet, rifle, posture) and leaves out the face, so one figure can stand for many.

screen.alt: The Memorial room: a soldier’s silhouette by a cross against the sunset, poppies in the field

steps.purpose: See the silhouette used again: a figure who stands for every soldier.
students: Why might the Memorial use the same figure, not a photograph of one man?

steps.title: Three symbols
script: **Symbols.** The **poppy**: the poster says poppies were often the only living things that could grow in the churned soil of the battlefields, and that people wear them in November to remember. The **cross**: John McCrae’s poem *In Flanders Fields* tells of crosses, row on row, marking graves. The **helmet**: the Brodie’s wide brim and its outline, painted with sand or sawdust so it would not catch the light.

steps.purpose: Read the poppy, the cross and the helmet as symbols.
students: Which symbol would someone recognize without any words?
Why does a living flower suit remembering?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout; every level ends with a design in black, gray, white and one red.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Find the red on the two posters and say what it marks. Match each symbol to its meaning. Then design a remembrance card: a silhouette, one symbol and one red.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Analyze the palette and the focal point of one poster. Make three thumbnail sketches for a remembrance panel, then draw the strongest one larger and explain your choices.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Compare the composition of the two posters. Design a panel for those whose names we’ll never know, using silhouette and negative space, and write a short artist’s statement.

steps.purpose: Design for remembrance at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. Every level ends with a design of your own: black, gray, white and one red.

steps.title: Gallery walk
script: Lay the designs out and walk the room in silence for two minutes. Then ask: *where did your eye go first, and why?* Ask two students to say what their red marks.

screen.question: Where does your eye go first? Why?

steps.purpose: Look at each other’s designs as a viewer would.
students: Find the red in a classmate’s design. What does it mark?
Which design would make you stop and remember?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down; for the last, ask a Red Level designer to explain one choice.
